issues.legal_issue: A public authority’s cancellation of a tender process is not arbitrary or mala fide when the decision is supported by bona fide reasons and serves the public interest in obtaining a fair price for a public asset.
material_facts: The authority had issued letters of intent, but formal allotments were dependent on regulatory clearances that were not received for more than five years.
During the delay, the market value of the plots rose substantially above the value underlying the original tender process.
The successful bidder had paid only earnest money and had not paid the remaining premium.
Before cancelling the process and deciding to invite fresh tenders, the authority obtained legal advice that it could do so.
The challenge did not contain specific pleadings explaining how the cancellation was motivated by mala fides.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation was based on valid considerations, was not arbitrary or mala fide, and was justified by the public interest in obtaining a realistic price for valuable public property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 of the Constitution, judicial review of a tender decision examines the legality of the decision-making process, not the merits of the decision itself. A public authority may refuse a bid or discontinue a tender for good and sufficient reasons, including where the bid does not represent market value; disposal of public property must be fair and transparent. The Court relied on Meerut Development Authority v. Association of Management Studies (2009) 6 SCC 171, Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) 6 SCC 651, Tejas Constructions and Infrastructure (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Council, Sendhwa (2012) 6 SCC 464, Raunaq International Ltd. v. I.V.R. Construction Ltd. (1999) 1 SCC 492, and the distinction between administrative and contractual issues explained in Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500.

rule.if: public_tender_cancellation_challenged_in_public_law_review and (clearance_delay_materially_changed_market_conditions and authority_sought_a_fairer_price_for_public_asset) and cancellation_reasons_were_recorded and not specific_mala_fide_basis_was_pleaded

predicates.public_tender_cancellation_challenged_in: A bidder challenges a public authority’s cancellation of a tender process through public-law review.
predicates.clearance_delay_materially_changed_marke: Required clearances were delayed, and market conditions materially changed during that delay.
predicates.authority_sought_a_fairer_price_for_publ: The authority sought a price for the public asset that better reflected its current market value.
predicates.cancellation_reasons_were_recorded: The authority recorded reasons for cancelling the process before inviting fresh tenders.
predicates.specific_mala_fide_basis_was_pleaded: The challenger pleaded a specific factual basis for alleging that the cancellation was motivated by mala fides.

issues.definition: When a bidder challenges a public tender cancellation, recorded reasons tied to a materially changed market and a fairer price for a public asset, together with no specifically pleaded mala fide basis, mean the cancellation is not arbitrary or mala fide.

issues.legal_issue: Promissory estoppel does not prevent a public authority from withdrawing a representation when the claimant has not materially changed its position to its detriment and the withdrawal is supported by public interest.
material_facts: The bidder relied on a letter of intent that made formal allotment dependent on clearances and further formal steps.
The bidder paid earnest money but did not pay the substantial remaining premium, incur other expenses, assume liabilities, or take steps to implement the project before cancellation.
The value of the public plots had risen substantially during the prolonged delay, and the authority sought to obtain a price reflecting that value.
issues.conclusion: The bidder could not invoke promissory estoppel to prevent cancellation; it had not changed its position to its prejudice, and the public interest could justify the authority changing its position.
issues.legal_principle: A representation does not attract promissory estoppel where the claimant has not altered its position to its prejudice to an extent that makes enforcement necessary to do justice. A supervening public interest may outweigh individual equity and permit the Government to withdraw a representation. The Court relied on M.P. Mathur v. Union of India (2006) 13 SCC 706 and the distinction between administrative-law doctrines and contractual rights explained in Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500.

predicates.public_body_promise_claimed_as_estoppel: A claimant relies on a representation by a public body and seeks to prevent its withdrawal through promissory estoppel.
predicates.claimant_made_no_material_detrimental_ch: The claimant did not materially alter its position to its detriment in reliance on the representation.
predicates.public_interest_favours_withdrawal: The public interest favours the public body withdrawing the representation.

issues.definition: When a claimant invokes promissory estoppel against a public body but has made no material detrimental change of position and the public interest favours withdrawal, promissory estoppel does not prevent withdrawal.

issues.legal_issue: A letter of intent that leaves formal allotment dependent on clearances and subsequent formal steps does not, on those terms, create a concluded contract.
material_facts: The letters of intent stated that formal allotment would follow receipt of general regulatory clearance and that further individual clearances could also be required.
The applicable allotment rules reserved the authority’s power to accept or reject a bid and stated that payment of earnest money and an offered premium created no right or interest in the land.
The rules required approvals from statutory authorities and made allotment subject to approval by the authority’s board or competent authority.
No formal allotment letter or lease was issued, possession was not given, and the remaining premium was not paid before cancellation.
issues.conclusion: The letters of intent expressed an intention to enter into a contract after further formalities and did not create a concluded contract on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a letter of intent is a final acceptance creating a contract or merely expresses an intention to contract later depends on its terms. A letter that makes final allotment conditional on clearances and subsequent formalities ordinarily indicates that the contract is to be made later. The Court relied on Dresser Rand S.A. v. Bindal Agro Chem Ltd. (2006) 1 SCC 751 and Speech & Software Technologies (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Neos Interactive Ltd., and considered the allotment rules’ provisions reserving the right to reject bids and requiring statutory and board approvals.

predicates.writ_claim_relies_on_letter_of_intent: A claimant seeks to establish contractual rights in a writ proceeding by relying on a letter of intent.
predicates.letter_makes_final_allotment_conditional: The letter states that final allotment depends on receipt of required clearances.
predicates.letter_requires_later_formal_steps: The letter contemplates further formal steps before the parties’ arrangement becomes final.
predicates.formal_allotment_and_lease_were_not_comp: The authority did not issue a formal allotment or complete the contemplated lease before the dispute arose.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a letter of intent that conditions final allotment on clearances and later formal steps, and no formal allotment or lease is completed, the letter does not create a concluded contract.

issues.legal_issue: A writ proceeding ordinarily cannot provide a full adjudication or enforcement of contractual rights where the dispute has no public-law element and the existence of a contract is seriously contested.
material_facts: The bidder pursued a writ proceeding challenging the authority’s cancellation rather than bringing an ordinary civil claim for contractual relief.
The dispute over whether the letter of intent created a concluded contract was seriously contested.
The contractual dispute was not pleaded or argued to have a public-law element.
The authority’s cancellation decision was separately considered under public-law principles and was found not arbitrary or unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The bidder could not obtain full adjudication or enforcement of the disputed contractual claim through the writ proceeding and had chosen the discretionary public-law remedy instead of an ordinary civil remedy.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 provides public-law review of administrative action, not a full adjudication of contractual rights or ordinary relief for breach of contract. Where a contractual dispute has no public-law element and the existence of a contract is seriously disputed, the court should not assume a valid contract and ordinarily should leave the claimant to pursue the available civil remedy. The Court relied on Kisan Sehkari Chini Mills v. Vardan Linkers (2008) 12 SCC 500 and ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd., JT 2013 (10) SC 300.

predicates.contractual_claim_brought_in_writ_procee: A claimant seeks contractual relief through a writ proceeding.
predicates.no_public_law_element_in_contractual_dis: The contractual dispute does not involve a public-law element.
predicates.existence_of_contract_seriously_disputed: The parties seriously dispute whether a contract was formed.

issues.definition: When a contractual claim is brought in a writ proceeding, has no public-law element, and concerns a seriously disputed contract, the contractual rights ordinarily require a civil remedy.
